title: Niko Brothers Take On a Flooded Monaco Diesel Pusher Bought for $21,000
dek: The RV rescuers paid a stated $21,000 for a water-damaged Monaco coach, and its value depends on whether the engine and Allison stayed dry.

episodes.t: I Bought a FLOODED Monaco Diesel Pusher for $21,000… Let's Bring It Back to Life!
episodes.what: Niko Brothers show off a flooded Monaco diesel pusher they bought for $21,000 and set out to bring it back to life.

parts.part: Engine oil, coolant, fuel and all filters, plus a fuel-tank flush
parts.why: Flood procedure is to drain the crankcase, replace every filter, drain the fuel and flush the tank and lines.

parts.part: Allison transmission fluid and filter service (done twice)
parts.why: Water in the fluid wrecks clutches. The guidance is to drain, check, refill, then drain and refill again after a few hours.
Batteries that have been submerged are normally replaced.

parts.part: Onan diesel generator recondition or replacement
parts.why: The generator sits low in the chassis and has its own engine and electrics.

parts.part: Wiring, connectors, starter and alternator service
parts.why: Flooded wiring has to dry out, and corroded harnesses need replacing. Starters and alternators have to be cleaned and dried.

parts.part: Interior flooring, insulation and lower cabinetry
parts.why: Wet flooring and particle board in a flooded coach grow mold and have to come out.

time: Just started: one episode so far, posted October 17, 2026.

costs.note: The $21,000 purchase price is stated. All $11,800 of parts is an estimate, because the channel hasn't given any repair costs. Labor is $0 because the brothers do their own work. Auction fees, transport and any engine or transmission rebuild aren't included.

value.basis: Clean-title mid-2000s Monaco diesel pushers at dealers run about $62,000 to $70,000 (a 2006 Diplomat sold for $62,450; a 2005 Dynasty is asking $69,900). Taking 20 to 40 percent off that for a flood or rebuilt title, per HeyRV, gives about $36,000 to $56,000. This assumes a Diplomat- or Dynasty-class coach in running order. The year and model aren't confirmed.

2005 Monaco Dynasty 42 Diamond IV, 123,935 miles, Cummins ISL 400 hp, Allison, 4 slides (asking price)

verdict: Too early to call. At a stated $21,000, the brothers paid about a third of what a clean mid-2000s Monaco diesel pusher brings at a dealer. Even after a 20 to 40 percent hit for a flood title, an estimated resale of $36,000 to $56,000 leaves room for about $12,000 of parts and a profit. The bet only works if the water stayed below the drivetrain: a rebuilt Cummins or Allison would use up most of the margin. The build shows the basic gamble of a salvage diesel pusher. The coach is cheap, and the risk lives in the parts nobody can see until it runs.
body:
## The buy

Niko Brothers, the channel that buys RVs and trucks out of salvage auctions, put up a new project on October 17, 2026. The title says they bought "a FLOODED Monaco Diesel Pusher for $21,000" and plan to "bring it back to life" [1]. The $21,000 comes from the brothers themselves, so it counts as a stated price. The title doesn't say where the coach came from. The channel's usual source is Copart, but this file doesn't confirm which auction sold this unit or where. It also doesn't confirm the coach's model year or which Monaco line it is (Dynasty, Diplomat, Camelot, Signature and so on). The car field uses 2006 only as a placeholder, picked as the middle of the model years in the comparable listings below. It is not a reported figure.

The channel has several auction RVs going at the same time. Other recent videos cover a $3,100 diesel pusher, a 2012 Tiffin, a coach with a damaged roof and a wrecked RV. Those are separate vehicles and are left out of this file.

## The damage

The only damage the episode title describes is flooding [1]. It doesn't say how deep the water got or whether it was fresh or salt water. Those two facts decide most of the cost. A diesel pusher keeps nearly everything that matters low and at the back. The engine (usually a Cummins, sometimes a Caterpillar) and the Allison automatic transmission sit in the rear. The coach also has an onboard diesel generator, a bank of house and chassis batteries, an inverter and converter, and hydraulic or electric slide-out and leveling systems. A Monaco from this era is typical. One comparable 2005 Dynasty lists a 400 hp Cummins ISL, an Allison automatic, a 10 kW Onan Quiet Diesel generator and four slides [5].

Flood water does predictable damage to that hardware. NC State Extension's guide to reconditioning flooded diesel farm machinery sets out the steps:

- **Engine:** check the cylinders for water with a borescope, turn the engine over to push it out, drain and wash the crankcase, replace every filter, and change the oil again after a few hours of running [3].
- **Fuel system:** drain all the fuel, flush the tank, blow out the lines and pull the injectors to inspect them [3].
- **Transmission:** drain the fluid, check it for water or dirt, replace the filter, and drain and refill again after a few hours [3].
- **Electrical:** starters and alternators have to be cleaned and dried, ECUs and harnesses inspected, and corroded wiring replaced. The guide warns that "Electrical wiring must be allowed to dry out" [3].

An RV adds more to that list. The house side has its own wiring, appliances, flooring, insulation and particle-board cabinetry, and slide-out motors and hydraulic pumps often sit low in the chassis. Salt water makes all of it worse.

## The work and the parts

As of this writing, only the first episode exists [1]. So the parts list below is the minimum a flooded diesel pusher usually needs, and every cost on it is an estimate, not a figure from the channel. The main open questions are the engine and transmission. If water got into the cylinders or the Allison, a fluid flush may not be enough, and either unit could need a rebuild that costs several times the purchase price of the coach.

## The money

The stated buy-in is $21,000 [1]. Adding estimated parts brings the total to about $33,000. Shop labor is counted at zero because the brothers do their own work.

On the selling side, comparable clean-title Monacos from the mid-2000s still bring good money at dealers:

- A 2006 Monaco Diplomat 38PST with 67,539 miles and a Cummins sold on consignment at a Texas dealer for a $62,450 sale price [4].
- A 2005 Dynasty 42 Diamond IV with 123,935 miles is offered at $69,900 in Arizona [5].
- A 2006 Dynasty 42 Diamond IV is offered at $96,000 [6].

A flood history changes those numbers. HeyRV puts the loss for a rebuilt-title RV at "anywhere from 20% to 40% less" than a clean one [2]. Taking 20 to 40 percent off the roughly $60,000 to $75,000 the 2005 and 2006 comps point to gives a resale range of about $36,000 to $56,000. That range assumes the coach turns out to be a mid-2000s Diplomat- or Dynasty-class unit. A Camelot or Knight sits lower, a Signature higher. The range is also only reachable if the drivetrain survived.

## What's next

The next episodes should answer the questions that decide the money: what year and model the coach is, how high the water got, whether the Cummins or Cat turns over cleanly, whether the Allison fluid comes out milky, and whether the generator and slides work. If the engine and transmission only need fluids and filters, $21,000 for a big Monaco leaves a lot of room. If either needs a rebuild, the margin shrinks quickly.
